story: After a great flood, humanity was left without guidance, which led to the rise of Adapa, a mortal man and sage or priest of the temple of Ea in the city of Eridu. Ea, sometimes considered his father, had given Adapa great wisdom but not eternal life. While carrying out his duties, Adapa was fishing on the river Tigris when the sea became rough from a strong wind and his boat capsized. Angered, Adapa broke the wings of the south wind, preventing it from blowing for seven days. The god Anu called Adapa to account for this action, but Ea instructed Adapa to gain the sympathy of Dumuzid and Gishzida, who guard the gates of heaven, and warned him not to eat or drink anything offered there, as it might kill him, but to accept and wear any garments and oil offered. Adapa put on mourning garments and told Dumuzid and Gishzida he mourned because they had disappeared from the land. He was then offered the food of life and water of life but refused them. When garments and oil were offered, he accepted and used them as instructed. Brought before Anu, he was asked why he refused to eat or drink, and he replied that Ea had told him not to. Anu laughed at Ea's actions and passed judgment, asking rhetorically what harm Adapa had brought on mankind, adding that men would now suffer disease, which the goddess Ninkarrak might relieve. Adapa was then sent back down to earth. The ending of the story is missing. In another fragmentary tale, Adapa and King Enmerkar descend nine cubits into the earth and break into an ancient tomb; what occurs there is unclear, but they leave and reseal the tomb.
